Definition: Whether government taxes, customs duties, and other revenue can be paid using the instant digital payment system, indicating integration of payment infrastructure with tax administration systems.
Comments: No credible evidence in saved materials on revenue model/fee caps/interchange or documented sustainability of national payment infrastructure (switch/instant system). Value set to unknown/NA.

revision_notes: Light check (fast path) surfaced an authoritative primary source (Ministry of Finance and Budget official website), so the row was moved to the full path. The E-PAY platform (launched October 2019) allows customs duties, taxes and other government charges (e.g. electricity bills) to be paid via mobile money, bank card and net banking; the FOUTA platform (piloted July 2026) is now consolidating this into a Treasury Single Account with phased rollout to all taxpayers by end-2026. Score raised from 0 (Unknown) to 3 (Yes).
revised_comments: Congo's Ministry of Finance and Budget operates the E-PAY platform, launched in October 2019, which enables taxpayers and importers to pay taxes and customs duties online using mobile money (MTN Mobile Money, Airtel Money), bank cards and net banking. Since July 2026 the ministry has been piloting FOUTA, a new online payment platform that centralises tax and duty collection and feeds into the Treasury Single Account, with phased rollout to all taxpayers due to be completed by the end of 2026. Government revenue collection is therefore integrated with digital payment infrastructure.

The extent to which these disbursements run through a national instant payment system rather than conventional banking or NGO-administered channels is unclear.

Comments: [Adjusted from 1 to 0: no source URL available] No specific payments consumer protection law/regulation (error resolution, chargebacks, mandated disclosure, dedicated ombuds) found in prior saved findings; treat as limited/unclear.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced BEAC's 2024 CEMAC payment services report, which is authoritative for Congo as a CEMAC member state. It confirms Governor's Instruction N°001/GR/2024 (22 January 2024) sets binding technical standards for electronic payment instruments across CEMAC, including transaction authentication and mandatory complaint/notification handling procedures, alongside COBAC's IT risk-management regulation (R-2024/01). This is sectoral/regional regulation addressing some consumer protection aspects of payments, not a dedicated national payment consumer protection law. Score raised from 0 to 2 (Partial).
revised_comments: As a member of the Central African Economic and Monetary Community (CEMAC), the Republic of Congo is subject to regional payment services regulation issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC) and the Central African Banking Commission (COBAC). The Governor's Instruction N°001/GR/2024 of 22 January 2024 sets technical standards for electronic payment instruments, including transaction authentication and complaint/notification-handling procedures, and COBAC's Regulation R-2024/01 (December 2024) addresses IT risk management at supervised payment institutions. These regional instruments provide partial, sector-specific consumer protection coverage for digital payments, rather than a dedicated national consumer protection law for payments.

revised_comments: The Republic of Congo hosts over 65,000 refugees and asylum seekers, mainly from the Central African Republic and the Democratic Republic of Congo, within a protection environment that grants access to social services, the labour market and the judicial system without restrictions on movement. Since 2021 the World Bank-funded Lisungi social safety net project has been extended to refugee-hosting areas such as Likouala, delivering quarterly conditional cash transfers to refugee families alongside host communities: 550 refugee families received transfers in Moungoungui, and 2,162 refugee households benefited from conditional cash transfers in 2023. This indicates partial, programme-based access to cash transfer mechanisms for refugees rather than confirmed universal legal access to standard digital payment accounts.
